subject: pathology
title: Leukocyte Phagocytosis, Respiratory Burst, and Genetic Adhesion Defects

steps.tx: Once leukocytes arrive at the focus of infection, they recognize, engulf, and degrade microbial invaders through phagocytosis. Efficient **leukocyte phagocytosis** involves three sequential steps: recognition and attachment of the target particle, engulfment by pseudopods to form a phagocytic vacuole, and destruction of the ingested microbe within the phagolysosome.
steps.say: Phagocytosis involves target particle recognition, pseudopod engulfment, and enzymatic degradation.

nodes.label: Opsonins (IgG Antibodies, Complement C3b) Coat Microbial Surface
Leukocyte Fc-Gamma and CR1 Receptors Bind Opsonized Foreign Target
Actin Polymerization Extends Pseudopodia Around Target, Sealing Phagosome
Primary Lysosomes Fuse with Phagosome to Form Hydrolytic Phagolysosome

steps.tx: While unopsonized microbes can be recognized directly by toll-like receptors and mannose receptors, phagocytic efficiency increases hundreds-fold when microbes are coated by host serum proteins termed opsonins. The most potent **endogenous opsonins** include immunoglobulin G antibodies binding via their Fc fragments, complement fragment C3b, and circulating collectins like mannose-binding lectin.
steps.say: Opsonization by IgG antibodies and complement C3b enhances phagocytosis hundreds of times.

left.title: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) Opsonin
points: Antigen-binding Fab arms coat specific microbial surface epitopes
Exposed constant Fc domain binds high-affinity Fc-gamma-RI (CD64)
Cross-linking of Fc receptors activates ITAM tyrosine kinase cascades
Triggers robust actin remodeling and immediate phagocytic engulfment

right.title: Complement Component C3b Opsonin
points: Generated during classical, lectin, or alternative complement cascades
Covalently bonds to microbial cell surface carbohydrates via thioester bond
Binds complement receptor-1 (CR1, CD35) on neutrophil membranes
Promotes particle adherence and synergistic phagocytic engulfment

steps.tx: Following target ingestion into a phagosome, the leukocyte unleashes a burst of oxygen consumption to generate lethal reactive oxygen species. Known as the **respiratory burst**, this rapid metabolic surge is catalyzed by the multi-protein enzyme complex nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase, which transfers electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen.
steps.say: The respiratory burst uses NADPH oxidase to reduce molecular oxygen into toxic superoxide radicals.

nodes.label: Ingestion Signals Translocation of Cytosolic Subunits (p47, p67) to Membrane
Assembles Active NADPH Oxidase Complex at Phagolysosomal Membrane
Transfers Electrons from NADPH to Oxygen, Generating Superoxide Anions (O2-)
Superoxide Dismutase Spontaneously Converts Superoxide into Hydrogen Peroxide

steps.tx: Within the primary azurophilic granules of neutrophils, a heme-containing green enzyme converts hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid in the presence of chloride ions. This powerful enzyme is **myeloperoxidase**, whose reaction product hypochlorous acid represents the active germicidal compound in household bleach, destroying bacterial proteins within milliseconds.
steps.say: Myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride to produce bactericidal hypochlorous acid.

left.title: MPO-H2O2-Halide Mechanism
points: Myeloperoxidase stored abundantly in neutrophil primary azurophilic granules
Utilizes H2O2 from NADPH oxidase and physiological chloride ions (Cl-)
Generates hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a lethal oxidizing and chlorinating agent
Most potent bactericidal killing mechanism in human neutrophils

right.title: Oxygen-Independent Killing
points: Lysozyme: hydrolyzes glycopeptide bonds of bacterial peptidoglycan walls
Defensins: cationic arginine-rich peptides that punch holes in microbial membranes
Lactoferrin: chelates nutritional iron, starving microbes of essential cofactor
Major basic protein: cytotoxic eosinophilic granule protein targeting helminths

steps.tx: Neutrophils that can eat but cannot kill define this disease. In **chronic granulomatous disease**, the NADPH oxidase complex fails, so phagosomes fill with living catalase positive bacteria and fungi that the cell cannot digest. Recurrent abscesses and granulomas in a young boy are the classic presentation. Prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals, and interferon in some centres, stand in for the missing burst.
steps.say: In chronic granulomatous disease the oxidase burst fails, leaving catalase positive organisms alive inside neutrophils. Recurrent abscesses and granulomas follow.

vis.alt: Image showing chronic granulomatous disease, neutrophils unable to kill ingested bacteria.
vis.caption: Bacteria survive inside a neutrophil whose oxidative burst has failed. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Congenital genetic mutations affecting components of the NADPH oxidase complex abolish reactive oxygen production, producing chronic granulomatous disease. Patients with **chronic granulomatous disease** cannot generate hydrogen peroxide, leaving them vulnerable to recurrent life-threatening infections by catalase-positive bacteria and fungi such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
steps.say: Chronic granulomatous disease lacks NADPH oxidase, leading to infections by catalase-positive bacteria.

vis.caption: Fungal hyphal proliferation demonstrating susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms like Aspergillus.
vis.alt: Pulmonary aspergillosis infection illustrating fungal invasion in impaired immunity

steps.tx: Catalase-positive microbes break down endogenous microbial hydrogen peroxide, denying neutrophils any substrate for myeloperoxidase-mediated hypochlorous acid synthesis. In contrast, catalase-negative bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae produce hydrogen peroxide that **leukocytes utilize against them**, allowing patients with chronic granulomatous disease to kill catalase-negative microbes normally.
steps.say: Catalase-negative streptococci produce their own hydrogen peroxide, which host MPO uses to kill them.

left.title: Catalase-Positive Pathogens (Lethal in CGD)
points: Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens
Nocardia species and Aspergillus fungal species
Endogenous bacterial catalase destroys bacterial H2O2 metabolic byproduct
Host neutrophils cannot form HOCl, leading to chronic granuloma formation

right.title: Catalase-Negative Pathogens (Killed in CGD)
points: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes
Lack catalase; produce and excrete H2O2 into the phagolysosome
Host myeloperoxidase borrows microbial H2O2 to generate lethal HOCl
CGD patients clear streptococcal infections with normal efficiency

steps.tx: Autosomal recessive mutations in the ITGB2 gene encoding the common beta-two integrin subunit CD18 cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type one. In **leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1**, neutrophils fail to express functional LFA-one and Mac-one, rendering them incapable of firm endothelial adhesion and extravasation into inflamed tissues.
steps.say: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 lacks CD18 integrins, preventing neutrophil extravasation into tissues.

nodes.label: Recessive Loss-of-Function Mutation in ITGB2 Gene on Chromosome 21q22
Complete Failure of Beta-2 Integrin Heterodimer Assembly (CD11a/CD18)
Neutrophils Roll on Selectins but Cannot Achieve Stable Firm Arrest
Presents with Delayed Umbilical Cord Separation and Absent Pus in Infections

steps.tx: The newborn clue is a cord stump that simply will not leave. **Delayed separation of the umbilical cord** beyond three weeks, with omphalitis and wounds that produce no pus, is the classic first announcement of leukocyte adhesion deficiency. Neutrophils crowd the bloodstream in huge numbers yet cannot stick, roll out or arrive, so infections rage undefended by the very cells meant to fight them. The paradox of sky high counts with absent pus teaches the whole adhesion cascade more memorably than any diagram of selectins alone.
steps.say: Delayed umbilical cord separation with pus free infections announces leukocyte adhesion deficiency in newborns.

vis.alt: Delayed separation of the umbilical cord in leukocyte adhesion deficiency
vis.caption: Delayed separation of the umbilical cord in leukocyte adhesion deficiency. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Because neutrophils cannot migrate across vascular walls into infected tissues, patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency type one present with a pathognomonic clinical triad. Affected infants display **delayed separation of the umbilical cord**, recurrent necrotic soft-tissue infections devoid of pus formation despite extreme peripheral blood neutrophilic leukocytosis.
steps.say: LAD-1 causes delayed umbilical cord separation, extreme leukocytosis, and infections without pus.
